> HackClock GT is a WiFi alarm clock built into a hypercar-shaped 3D-printed case, with a 7-segment time display on the windshield and a TFT screen in the left door. It pulls in weather, stocks, and news, plays alarms through a Bluetooth speaker, and works with a voice assistant through Home Assistant, with a watch charger on the roof and a pressable spoiler to snooze or stop alarms.

## Design

### 2026-11-01: I started by deciding what my clock should look like. I wanted a low, wide hypercar with a big windshield that could hold the time display, and I wanted the body to hide a lot of electronics. I built

**7h**

I started by deciding what my clock should look like. I wanted a low, wide hypercar with a big windshield that could hold the time display, and I wanted the body to hide a lot of electronics. I built the case on the computer piece by piece. I began with a side profile for the lower body, then added angled cabin panels for the windshield, roof and rear, and then the hood and nose. I learned that building it in separate pieces makes changes easy, because I can move something like the roof pocket without redoing the rest of the car.

The body has a nose with headlight slots, a hood, a cabin with a windshield and side windows, a roof pocket sized for my own Samsung watch charger, and a tail with a USB-C power slot and a USB-A slot. The wheels, windshield and side glass are separate parts, so I can print them in black and smoky plastic. I also learned that wheel arches and flared fenders are the hardest part to get watertight, because the flare has to close up cleanly where it meets the body.

The most important thing I learned this entry was to check the model before printing. I made a checker that makes sure every part is a closed, watertight solid with all the faces pointing outward. A model with holes in it slices badly and prints worse, and I fixed several flipped faces this way.

### 2026-11-01: At first the rear spoiler was only for looks, but then I realized it could be my main button. It is a separate printed wing that sits on two hinge pins and rests on a small switch hidden underneath. W

**4h**

At first the rear spoiler was only for looks, but then I realized it could be my main button. It is a separate printed wing that sits on two hinge pins and rests on a small switch hidden underneath. When I slap the wing down, it presses the switch and stops or snoozes the alarm. I think this is way better than hunting for a tiny button first thing in the morning, and it fits a car.

Building it took a few parts. I made two struts with pin holes, a hollow switch pedestal on the rear deck, and a slot so the switch wires can run down into the body. The hinge pin is just a piece of filament scrap, so it costs nothing. The pedestal holds the switch at the right height, but I learned that I may need a thin shim under the switch after I measure the real part. I also learned that a wing prints best upside down, because then it needs no support material, so my export flips it and my pictures flip it back.

I also simplified the controls. I removed the UP and DOWN buttons, because the time comes from the internet and I set alarms from my phone or by voice. I moved MODE and TALK to the left door, right next to the screen, as small panel buttons. That left only three controls, and the front looks much cleaner.

### 2026-11-01: I split the electronics across two boards, because the parts need different chips. A XIAO ESP32-S3 runs the clock, the screens, the WiFi and the alarms. A classic ESP32 WROVER-E handles Bluetooth audi

**5h**

I split the electronics across two boards, because the parts need different chips. A XIAO ESP32-S3 runs the clock, the screens, the WiFi and the alarms. A classic ESP32 WROVER-E handles Bluetooth audio and voice, because I learned that the S3 chip cannot act as a Bluetooth speaker. The two boards talk over a shared I2C bus, along with the 7-segment display and the real-time clock chip, and each device has its own address so they do not collide.

I made my circuit board as a KiCad file. It is a small two layer board with labeled headers for the screen, the displays, the clock chip, the microphone, the amplifier, the buttons, the buzzers and USB-C. The copper traces were routed automatically, and I had to retry the routing several times before every connection fit. I also drew the schematics for both boards and wrote a wiring guide that says exactly which wire goes where.

All the buttons share one analog pin through a ladder of resistors, and each button pulls the pin to a different voltage. I kept that design so the board did not have to change when I took buttons away. I learned a lot about how one pin can read many buttons just by measuring voltage. I also opened the board in KiCad to make sure it loads.

### 2026-11-01: So basically my firmware gets the time from the internet and uses a battery clock chip as a backup. It shows the weather, stock prices and news headlines on the door screen, and it shows the time on t

**5h**

So basically my firmware gets the time from the internet and uses a battery clock chip as a backup. It shows the weather, stock prices and news headlines on the door screen, and it shows the time on the windshield display. I made a settings page at hackclock.local so I can change alarms, volume, brightness and time zone from my phone. For first-time setup, the clock opens a WiFi portal called HackClock-Setup, so I never have to type my WiFi password into the code

Buttons needed extra thought now that there are only three. I sort every press into a short press, a long press, a repeat, or a very long press, so one button can do several jobs. Slapping the spoiler stops an alarm, MODE snoozes it, and holding MODE for a very long time makes the clock forget the WiFi. Holding MODE for a shorter time changes the brightness.

I made a final render of the whole car with every part in place, including the screens, speaker, boards, wires, watch charger and spoiler button. It shows what the finished clock will look like

![finalcarpicture](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/Av04i46we8M37lS6usKkrddBHAP0IRTt/4e224eeb30bf72ca44c8b5ecfcd3c95178486011a58a797953750c65142e6d11.png)
The audio board plays Bluetooth music under the name HackClock, plays spoken answers through the amplifier, and sends my voice to Home Assistant for the wake word and commands. I learned how to split work between two chips and keep them talking to each other. I learned that a clock needs a plan for when the internet fails, which is why the backup clock chip matters.
